name: Dry, gritty eyes
summary: Dry eyes happen when your eyes do not make enough tears or the tears dry up too quickly. Eyes can feel gritty, burning or sore, and are often worse with screens, wind or air conditioning.
redFlags: Sudden changes to your sight, such as wavy lines, flashing or loss of vision
It hurts to look at light
A red eye with a severe headache and feeling sick
An injury to the eye, or something stuck in it
urgentFlags: Your eye is painful and red
You have a red eye and wear contact lenses

commonCauses.title: Screen use and environment
commonCauses.detail: Blinking less while using screens, plus wind, heating or air conditioning, can dry the eyes.

commonCauses.title: Ageing and hormonal changes
commonCauses.detail: Dry eyes become more common with age and around the menopause.

commonCauses.title: Blepharitis
commonCauses.detail: Inflamed eyelids can affect the oily layer of the tears.

commonCauses.title: Contact lenses and medicines
commonCauses.detail: Contact lenses and some medicines, such as antihistamines, can dry the eyes.

commonCauses.title: Other conditions
commonCauses.detail: Conditions such as Sjögren's syndrome or thyroid eye disease can cause dry eyes.

selfCare: Ask a pharmacist about lubricating eye drops, gels or ointments
Take regular screen breaks and remember to blink
Keep eyelids clean and use a warm compress if they are crusty
Use a humidifier or keep rooms well ventilated
Wear wraparound glasses outdoors in wind
avoid: Smoky, dry or windy places where possible
Rubbing your eyes
Wearing contact lenses for long periods while eyes are dry
seeDoctorIf: Dry eyes have not improved after a few weeks of home treatment
There is any change in the shape of your eyelids
You also have a dry mouth or joint pain

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology – What is dry eye?

name: Watery eyes
summary: Watery eyes are common and can be caused by irritation, allergies, dry eyes or blocked tear ducts. They often settle without treatment.
redFlags: Sudden loss of vision
A chemical has got into the eye
An injury that has pierced or cut the eye
urgentFlags: Any change to your vision
Severe eye pain
A watery eye that is very red and painful, or sensitive to light

commonCauses.title: Dry eyes
commonCauses.detail: Irritated dry eyes can make too many reflex tears.

commonCauses.title: Allergies and conjunctivitis
commonCauses.detail: Hay fever and eye infections cause watering, itching and redness.

commonCauses.title: Blocked tear duct
commonCauses.detail: Common in babies and older adults; tears cannot drain so they spill over.

commonCauses.title: Eyelid problems
commonCauses.detail: Eyelids turning in or out, or blepharitis, can cause watering.

commonCauses.title: Irritants
commonCauses.detail: Wind, cold, smoke or a speck of dust can make eyes water.

selfCare: Ask a pharmacist about eye drops for dryness or allergy
Hold a warm compress over closed eyes and gently massage the eyelids
Clean crusty eyelids with cooled boiled water
Protect your eyes from wind and cold with glasses
avoid: Rubbing your eyes
Smoky environments
seeDoctorIf: Your eyes keep watering and it is affecting everyday activities
Your eyelid is turning inwards or drooping away from the eye
You have lumps or swelling around the eyes that have not improved

name: Eyelid twitching
summary: A twitching eyelid is very common and almost always harmless. It is often linked to tiredness, stress, caffeine or eye strain and usually goes away on its own.
redFlags: Twitching with face drooping, weakness, numbness or slurred speech
A drooping eyelid that comes on suddenly with a severe headache or double vision
urgentFlags: The eyelid closes completely with each twitch and you cannot open it
Twitching with a red, painful eye or discharge

commonCauses.title: Tiredness and stress
commonCauses.detail: The most common triggers for a harmless eyelid twitch.

commonCauses.title: Caffeine and alcohol
commonCauses.detail: Too much coffee, tea, energy drinks or alcohol can trigger twitching.

commonCauses.title: Eye strain and dry eyes
commonCauses.detail: Long screen use and dry or irritated eyes can cause twitching.

commonCauses.title: Blepharospasm or hemifacial spasm
commonCauses.detail: Rare conditions causing persistent forced closing of the eyelids or twitching of one side of the face.

selfCare: Get more sleep and try to reduce stress
Cut down on caffeine and alcohol
Take regular breaks from screens
Use lubricating eye drops if your eyes feel dry
avoid: Rubbing or pressing on the eye
Supplements marketed as cures for eye twitching
seeDoctorIf: Twitching lasts more than a few weeks
Twitching spreads to other parts of your face
Your eyelid droops
The eye becomes red, swollen or has discharge

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology – Eyelid twitching

name: Double vision
summary: Double vision is when you see two images of a single object. It can come from a problem in one eye or from the eyes not lining up, and it should always be checked.
redFlags: Double or blurred vision with a severe headache or an enlarged pupil
Double vision after a head injury
Double vision with face drooping, weakness, numbness, slurred speech or loss of balance
A drooping eyelid that started suddenly with double vision
urgentFlags: Double vision that has started suddenly
Double vision with eye pain

commonCauses.title: Eye surface or lens problems
commonCauses.detail: Dry eyes, astigmatism or cataracts can cause a ghost image in one eye.

commonCauses.title: Squint or eye muscle problems
commonCauses.detail: When the eyes do not line up, each sees a slightly different image.

commonCauses.title: Nerve problems
commonCauses.detail: Diabetes, high blood pressure or other conditions can affect the nerves that move the eyes.

commonCauses.title: Stroke, head injury or thyroid eye disease
commonCauses.detail: More serious causes that need prompt assessment.

selfCare: Cover one eye to check whether double vision is in one or both eyes, and tell the clinician
Do not drive until your vision has been checked
Take care on stairs and steps
avoid: Driving or operating machinery
Waiting to see if sudden double vision goes away
seeDoctorIf: You think you or your child might have double vision, even if it comes and goes
You have double vision when tired
You have diabetes or thyroid problems and notice vision changes

name: Sudden loss of vision
summary: Losing some or all of the sight in one or both eyes suddenly is an emergency, even if it comes back. Quick treatment can save sight and may reveal a stroke risk.
redFlags: Sudden loss of vision in one or both eyes, even if it has come back
A dark curtain or shadow moving across your vision
Sudden severe eye pain with vision loss
Vision loss with face drooping, weakness, numbness or slurred speech
Vision loss with a new headache and jaw pain or scalp tenderness
urgentFlags: Vision that is gradually getting worse over days
Patchy vision or blind spots that are new

commonCauses.title: Retinal detachment
commonCauses.detail: Often starts with flashes and floaters followed by a shadow over the vision.

commonCauses.title: Blocked blood vessel in the eye or stroke
commonCauses.detail: Can cause sudden painless loss of sight in one eye.

commonCauses.title: Giant cell arteritis
commonCauses.detail: Inflamed arteries, usually in people over 50, with headache and scalp tenderness.

commonCauses.title: Acute glaucoma or other eye conditions
commonCauses.detail: Can cause a painful red eye and blurred vision.

selfCare: Get emergency help straight away; note the time it started
Do not drive; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance
avoid: Waiting to see if vision returns
Rubbing or pressing on the eye
seeDoctorIf: You notice gradual changes in your vision
You have not had an eye test in the last 2 years

name: Swollen or drooping eyelid
summary: A swollen eyelid is often caused by an allergy, a stye, an insect bite or rubbing the eye. Swelling that is red, hot and painful, or that affects vision, needs to be seen quickly.
redFlags: Swelling of the eyelids with swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, or difficulty breathing
Red, swollen eyelid with fever, pain when moving the eye, a bulging eye or changes in vision
An eyelid that drooped suddenly with a severe headache, double vision, face drooping or weakness
urgentFlags: Your swollen eyelid is red, hot, painful, tender or blistered
Your eyelid droops suddenly
You cannot open your eye or keep it open
A newborn baby has a sticky, red, swollen eye

commonCauses.title: Allergy
commonCauses.detail: Hay fever, cosmetics or insect bites can cause puffy, itchy eyelids.

commonCauses.title: Stye or chalazion
commonCauses.detail: A lump on the eyelid with local swelling.

commonCauses.title: Blepharitis or conjunctivitis
commonCauses.detail: Inflammation of the eyelids or eye surface can cause swelling.

commonCauses.title: Fluid and sleep
commonCauses.detail: Puffy eyes in the morning are common and often linked to salt, alcohol or poor sleep.

commonCauses.title: Cellulitis around the eye
commonCauses.detail: A skin infection that needs urgent treatment, especially in children.

selfCare: Hold a cool compress over the closed eye
Ask a pharmacist about antihistamines if allergy is likely
Keep the eyelids clean
Raise your head with an extra pillow at night
avoid: Rubbing or squeezing the eyelid
Wearing make-up or contact lenses until the swelling settles
Using a product you suspect caused a reaction
seeDoctorIf: Eyelid symptoms are not improving after a few days
You keep getting swollen eyelids
Your eyelid has gradually started to droop
You have yellow patches or lumps around your eyes

name: Sensitivity to light
summary: Sensitivity to light means bright light causes discomfort or pain. It is common during migraines and with some eye problems, but with a red, painful eye or fever it can be a sign of something serious.
redFlags: Light sensitivity with a fever, stiff neck, severe headache or a rash that does not fade
Light sensitivity with a red eye, severe headache and feeling sick
Light sensitivity with sudden vision loss or after an eye injury
Light sensitivity with confusion or drowsiness
urgentFlags: Light sensitivity with a painful or red eye
Light sensitivity with blurred vision
Light sensitivity in a contact lens wearer

commonCauses.title: Migraine
commonCauses.detail: Many people need to avoid light during a migraine attack.

commonCauses.title: Dry eyes and eye strain
commonCauses.detail: Can make bright light uncomfortable.

commonCauses.title: Eye inflammation or infection
commonCauses.detail: Iritis, corneal scratches or infections can make light very painful.

commonCauses.title: Meningitis
commonCauses.detail: A rare but serious cause, with headache, fever and stiff neck.

selfCare: Wear sunglasses or a hat with a brim outdoors
Dim screens and lights, and rest in a darker room
Treat a known migraine as you usually would
avoid: Staying in complete darkness for long periods, which can increase sensitivity over time
Ignoring light sensitivity with a red, painful eye
seeDoctorIf: Light sensitivity keeps coming back
It is affecting your daily activities
You have frequent headaches with it

name: Eye injury or something in the eye
summary: Small specks of dust or grit can often be rinsed out with clean water. Chemicals in the eye, sharp or high-speed objects, and injuries that affect vision need emergency care.
redFlags: A strong chemical such as bleach or oven cleaner has got into the eye (keep rinsing with water while getting help)
A sharp object has pierced the eye, or something hit it at high speed
Any change in sight after an eye injury
Severe eye pain, or blood or pus coming from the eye
Cannot move the eye or keep it open
Headache, light sensitivity or being sick after an eye injury
urgentFlags: The injured eye is not getting better after 24 hours
The eye is very painful
A child has injured their eye
It still feels like something is in the eye after rinsing

commonCauses.title: Dust, grit or an eyelash
commonCauses.detail: Usually washes out with tears or clean water.

commonCauses.title: Scratch on the eye surface (corneal abrasion)
commonCauses.detail: Painful and watery, often healing within a few days.

commonCauses.title: Blunt injury
commonCauses.detail: A blow can cause a black eye or bleeding inside the eye.

commonCauses.title: Chemical splash
commonCauses.detail: Household or workplace chemicals can cause serious damage.

selfCare: Wash the eye with plenty of clean, lukewarm water
Follow the advice on the packaging if a household product gets in the eye
Hold a cold compress gently on a black eye
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if needed, following the pack instructions
Wear eye protection for DIY, gardening and power tools
avoid: Trying to remove anything stuck in the eye
Rubbing or pressing on the eye
Wearing contact lenses until the eye has healed
seeDoctorIf: Your eye remains irritated or watery after a few days
A black eye is not fading after 2 weeks

name: Eye strain or tired eyes
summary: Eye strain is tired, aching or burning eyes after long periods of close work, reading, driving or using screens. It is uncomfortable but does not damage the eyes, and usually settles with rest.
redFlags: Sudden loss or change of vision
Severe eye pain with a red eye, headache and feeling sick
urgentFlags: Eye pain with redness or sensitivity to light
New double vision

commonCauses.title: Screen use
commonCauses.detail: Focusing on screens reduces blinking and tires the eye muscles.

commonCauses.title: Uncorrected vision
commonCauses.detail: Needing glasses, or an out-of-date prescription, makes the eyes work harder.

commonCauses.title: Dry eyes and lighting
commonCauses.detail: Glare, poor lighting and dry air add to strain.

selfCare: Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds
Set screens about an arm's length away and slightly below eye level
Reduce glare and use good lighting
Use lubricating eye drops if your eyes feel dry
Have a sight test to check whether you need glasses
avoid: Using screens for hours without breaks
Reading in dim light
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms continue despite screen breaks
You have frequent headaches with eye strain
Your vision seems to be changing

sources.label: American Academy of Ophthalmology – Eye strain

name: Earache
summary: Earache is common, especially in children, and is often caused by an ear infection that gets better on its own within a few days. Pain can also come from the throat, teeth or jaw.
redFlags: Earache with a stiff neck, severe headache, drowsiness or a rash that does not fade
Earache with face drooping or sudden weakness of the face
Earache with a very swollen, red area behind the ear pushing the ear forward
Earache with confusion or being very unwell and difficult to wake
urgentFlags: Earache that has lasted more than 2 to 3 days
Very high temperature, or feeling hot and shivery
Swelling around the ear, or fluid coming out of the ear
Hearing loss or a change in hearing
Something stuck in the ear
A child under 2 with earache in both ears

commonCauses.title: Middle ear infection
commonCauses.detail: Often follows a cold; common in children and usually clears in 3 to 5 days.

commonCauses.title: Outer ear infection (otitis externa)
commonCauses.detail: Pain, itching and discharge, often after swimming.

commonCauses.title: Earwax or a blocked ear
commonCauses.detail: Can cause discomfort and muffled hearing.

commonCauses.title: Pain from nearby areas
commonCauses.detail: Sore throat, tonsillitis, toothache, teething or jaw joint problems can be felt in the ear.

selfCare: Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Hold a warm or cold flannel against the ear
Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Ask a pharmacist for advice; in some countries they can treat ear infections
avoid: Putting cotton buds, fingers or anything else in the ear
Getting the ear wet if it is infected or discharging
Using olive oil or drops if the eardrum might be burst
seeDoctorIf: You or your child keep getting earache
Earache does not improve after 3 days
You have diabetes or a weakened immune system and an ear infection

name: Discharge from the ear
summary: Fluid leaking from the ear is often caused by an ear infection or a perforated (burst) eardrum. It should be checked by a doctor or pharmacist.
redFlags: Clear fluid or blood from the ear after a head injury
Ear discharge with a stiff neck, severe headache, confusion or a rash that does not fade
Ear discharge with face drooping or sudden severe dizziness
urgentFlags: Ear discharge with a high temperature or feeling generally unwell
Swelling, redness or pain behind the ear
Ear discharge with hearing loss
Discharge after a loud bang or an injury to the ear

commonCauses.title: Middle ear infection with a perforated eardrum
commonCauses.detail: Pain often eases once pus drains; the eardrum usually heals within weeks.

commonCauses.title: Outer ear infection
commonCauses.detail: Itching, pain and discharge from the ear canal.

commonCauses.title: Earwax
commonCauses.detail: Soft wax can look like discharge.

commonCauses.title: Injury
commonCauses.detail: Damage to the ear canal or eardrum from cotton buds or loud noise.

selfCare: Wipe away discharge from the outer ear with clean cotton wool
Keep the ear dry: avoid swimming and cover the ear in the shower
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if needed, following the pack instructions
avoid: Poking cotton buds or anything else into the ear
Using ear drops not recommended by a doctor or pharmacist if the eardrum may be burst
Swimming until the ear has healed
seeDoctorIf: You have any ear discharge that has not been checked
Discharge keeps coming back
Hearing has not returned to normal after the infection clears

name: Ringing in the ears (tinnitus)
summary: Tinnitus is hearing sounds such as ringing, buzzing or humming that do not come from outside. It is common, often linked to hearing loss or loud noise, and is rarely a sign of something serious.
redFlags: Tinnitus after a head injury
Tinnitus with sudden hearing loss
Tinnitus with weakness of the face muscles
Tinnitus with a sudden spinning sensation (vertigo)
urgentFlags: Tinnitus that beats in time with your pulse
Tinnitus in one ear only that came on recently

commonCauses.title: Age-related hearing loss
commonCauses.detail: Tinnitus often comes with gradual hearing loss.

commonCauses.title: Loud noise
commonCauses.detail: Concerts, loud music or noisy work can cause short-term or lasting tinnitus.

commonCauses.title: Earwax or ear infection
commonCauses.detail: A blocked or infected ear can cause ringing that goes once treated.

commonCauses.title: Ménière's disease
commonCauses.detail: Tinnitus with attacks of vertigo, hearing loss and ear fullness.

commonCauses.title: Stress, anxiety and some medicines
commonCauses.detail: These can make tinnitus more noticeable.

selfCare: Use soft background sound, such as a fan or quiet music, especially at bedtime
Try relaxation, deep breathing or yoga to reduce stress
Keep a regular bedtime routine and cut down on caffeine
Protect your ears from loud noise with earplugs
Join a tinnitus support group
avoid: Complete silence, which can make tinnitus more noticeable
Loud noise without ear protection
Supplements or devices claiming to cure tinnitus
seeDoctorIf: You have tinnitus regularly or constantly
It is getting worse
It is affecting your sleep, concentration or mood
You also have hearing loss

name: Hearing loss (gradual)
summary: Gradual hearing loss is common, especially with age or after years of loud noise. Some causes, like earwax or an infection, are easily treated, so it is worth getting your hearing checked.
redFlags: Hearing loss after a head injury
Hearing loss with face drooping, weakness, slurred speech or severe vertigo
urgentFlags: Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears
Hearing getting worse over days or weeks
Hearing loss with earache or discharge from the ear

commonCauses.title: Ageing
commonCauses.detail: Gradual hearing loss in both ears is very common as people get older.

commonCauses.title: Noise damage
commonCauses.detail: Years of exposure to loud noise can damage the inner ear.

commonCauses.title: Earwax build-up
commonCauses.detail: Can cause muffled hearing, usually in one ear.

commonCauses.title: Ear infection or glue ear
commonCauses.detail: Fluid behind the eardrum reduces hearing, especially in children.

selfCare: Try an online or pharmacy hearing test
Ask people to face you and speak clearly; reduce background noise
Use ear drops for wax only if a pharmacist says they are suitable
Protect your ears from loud noise
avoid: Using cotton buds or ear candles to remove wax
Listening to loud music through headphones for long periods
seeDoctorIf: You think your hearing is getting worse
Hearing has not come back after treatment for wax or an infection
Hearing loss is in one ear only
You are worried about a child's hearing or speech

name: Sudden hearing loss
aliases: woke up deaf in one ear
summary: Hearing loss that comes on over hours or a few days needs to be checked quickly, because some types are more treatable when treatment starts early. A blocked ear from wax or a cold is a common harmless cause.
redFlags: Sudden hearing loss with face drooping, weakness, numbness or slurred speech
Sudden hearing loss with severe vertigo and inability to walk
Hearing loss after a head injury
urgentFlags: Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears without an obvious cause like a cold or wax
Sudden hearing loss with ringing or a feeling of fullness in the ear
Hearing loss after a loud bang or an injury to the ear

commonCauses.title: Earwax or a cold
commonCauses.detail: A blocked ear can cause sudden muffled hearing.

commonCauses.title: Ear infection or perforated eardrum
commonCauses.detail: Usually with pain or discharge.

commonCauses.title: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss
commonCauses.detail: Damage to the inner ear or hearing nerve, often with no clear cause; early treatment can help.

commonCauses.title: Inner ear conditions
commonCauses.detail: Ménière's disease or labyrinthitis can affect hearing and balance.

selfCare: Get an urgent appointment rather than waiting for it to clear
Note when it started and any other symptoms such as dizziness or ringing
avoid: Assuming it is just wax and waiting several days
Putting objects or home remedies in the ear
seeDoctorIf: Hearing has not fully returned after a cold or ear infection
You keep getting episodes of reduced hearing

name: Blocked ear or ear wax
summary: A blocked feeling in the ear is often caused by earwax, a cold, or pressure changes when flying. It usually clears on its own or with simple treatment.
redFlags: Blocked ear with sudden face drooping, weakness or slurred speech
Blocked ear after a head injury with fluid coming out
urgentFlags: Sudden hearing loss not explained by a cold or wax
Severe ear pain, high temperature or discharge
Something stuck in the ear

commonCauses.title: Earwax build-up
commonCauses.detail: Wax can build up and cause muffled hearing, itching or ringing.

commonCauses.title: Colds and sinus congestion
commonCauses.detail: Swelling blocks the tube between the ear and the back of the nose.

commonCauses.title: Pressure changes
commonCauses.detail: Flying, diving or driving in mountains can cause a blocked, popping ear.

commonCauses.title: Ear infection or glue ear
commonCauses.detail: Fluid in the middle ear causes fullness and reduced hearing.

selfCare: Ask a pharmacist about ear drops or olive oil drops to soften wax, if your eardrum is not damaged
Lie with the affected ear upwards for a few minutes after putting drops in
Swallow, yawn or chew gum to help an ear pop after flying
Gently breathe out with your mouth closed while pinching your nose to clear pressure
avoid: Using cotton buds, fingers or objects to clean inside the ear
Ear candles, which do not work and can cause burns
Using ear drops if you have had a perforated eardrum or ear surgery, unless advised
seeDoctorIf: Earwax symptoms have not cleared after 5 days of drops
Your ear is badly blocked and you cannot hear
You keep getting blocked ears

name: Itchy ears
summary: Itchy ears are usually caused by dry skin, eczema, earwax or a mild outer ear infection. They are rarely serious.
redFlags: Itching with sudden swelling of the face, lips or tongue and difficulty breathing
urgentFlags: Itching with severe pain, swelling around the ear or a high temperature
Discharge from the ear with hearing loss
You have diabetes or a weakened immune system and a painful, itchy ear

commonCauses.title: Dry skin or eczema
commonCauses.detail: The skin in the ear canal can become dry, flaky and itchy.

commonCauses.title: Outer ear infection
commonCauses.detail: Itching, pain and discharge, often after swimming or cleaning the ears.

commonCauses.title: Earwax
commonCauses.detail: A build-up of wax can feel itchy.

commonCauses.title: Allergy
commonCauses.detail: Reactions to earrings, hearing aids, earphones or hair products.

selfCare: Keep ears dry after swimming or showering by tilting your head
Ask a pharmacist about suitable ear drops
Clean earphones and hearing aids regularly
Avoid products that seem to cause a reaction
avoid: Scratching inside the ear with cotton buds, fingers or pins
Ear candles
seeDoctorIf: Itching does not improve after a week of self-care
You develop pain or discharge
Itching keeps coming back

name: Blocked or stuffy nose
summary: A blocked nose is usually caused by a cold, hay fever or sinusitis and gets better on its own. A nose blocked on one side only for weeks should be checked.
redFlags: Swelling around the eyes with fever, vision changes or difficulty moving the eye
A blocked nose with a severe headache, stiff neck, confusion or a rash that does not fade
Difficulty breathing (not just a blocked nose)
urgentFlags: Feeling very unwell or getting worse despite self-care
Severe pain in the face or forehead that painkillers do not help
You have a weakened immune system

commonCauses.title: Common cold
commonCauses.detail: Viral infection with a blocked or runny nose that improves within 1 to 2 weeks.

commonCauses.title: Allergies
commonCauses.detail: Hay fever, dust mites or pets can cause a blocked, itchy, sneezy nose.

commonCauses.title: Sinusitis
commonCauses.detail: Inflamed sinuses causing a blocked nose, facial pain and reduced smell.

commonCauses.title: Nasal polyps or a deviated septum
commonCauses.detail: Can cause long-term blockage, often worse on one side.

selfCare: Rinse your nose with a saltwater (saline) spray or rinse
Breathe in steam, for example in a warm shower
Raise your head with an extra pillow at night
Ask a pharmacist about decongestants or antihistamines that suit you
Rest and drink plenty of fluids
avoid: Using decongestant nasal sprays for more than about a week, as they can make congestion worse
Smoking and smoky rooms
Antibiotics for a cold, which do not work against viruses
seeDoctorIf: Your blocked nose has lasted more than 3 weeks
It is only ever blocked on one side
You have nosebleeds or bloody discharge with it
You keep getting sinusitis

name: Runny nose and sneezing
summary: A runny nose and sneezing are usually caused by a cold or an allergy such as hay fever. They are rarely serious and usually settle with time and simple care.
redFlags: Sneezing or runny nose with swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, wheezing or difficulty breathing
Clear watery fluid from the nose after a head injury
urgentFlags: Feeling very unwell with a very high temperature
Symptoms suddenly getting worse after starting to improve
Shortness of breath or chest pain with a cold

commonCauses.title: Common cold
commonCauses.detail: A viral infection that usually gets better within 1 to 2 weeks.

commonCauses.title: Hay fever and other allergies
commonCauses.detail: Sneezing, itchy eyes and a runny nose triggered by pollen, dust or pets.

commonCauses.title: Non-allergic rhinitis
commonCauses.detail: Runny nose triggered by things like cold air, spicy food or strong smells.

commonCauses.title: Flu or COVID-19
commonCauses.detail: Usually with fever, aches and tiredness.

selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Use saltwater nasal sprays or rinses
Ask a pharmacist about antihistamines for allergy symptoms
Wash your hands often and catch sneezes in a tissue
On high-pollen days, keep windows closed and shower after being outside
avoid: Antibiotics for a cold
Overusing decongestant sprays
Unproven remedies such as high-dose vitamin supplements to cure a cold
seeDoctorIf: Symptoms do not improve after 3 weeks
Allergy symptoms are not controlled by pharmacy treatments
You have a long-term condition such as asthma and symptoms are affecting it

name: Nosebleed
summary: Nosebleeds are common and usually not serious. Most stop with simple first aid within 10 to 15 minutes.
redFlags: The nosebleed lasts longer than 10 to 15 minutes despite pressure
The bleeding seems very heavy
Swallowing a large amount of blood that makes you vomit
The bleeding started after a blow to the head
Feeling weak, dizzy or faint
Difficulty breathing
urgentFlags: A nosebleed in someone taking blood-thinning medicine
A nosebleed in someone with a bleeding disorder such as haemophilia
A nosebleed after an injury to the nose that may be broken

commonCauses.title: Picking or blowing the nose
commonCauses.detail: The blood vessels inside the front of the nose are delicate and easily damaged.

commonCauses.title: Dry air
commonCauses.detail: A dry nose from heating or changes in temperature cracks and bleeds more easily.

commonCauses.title: Colds and allergies
commonCauses.detail: Inflammation and frequent blowing make bleeding more likely.

commonCauses.title: Injury, medicines or blood conditions
commonCauses.detail: Blood thinners, a broken nose or clotting problems can cause heavier bleeding.

selfCare: Sit down and lean forward, not back
Pinch the soft part of your nose just above the nostrils firmly for 10 to 15 minutes
Breathe through your mouth and spit out any blood
Hold an ice pack wrapped in a cloth on the bridge of the nose
Once stopped, avoid blowing or picking your nose and avoid hot drinks and heavy lifting for 24 hours
avoid: Tilting your head back, which makes you swallow blood
Lying down during a nosebleed
Picking or blowing your nose straight afterwards
seeDoctorIf: You have regular nosebleeds
A child under 2 has had a nosebleed
You have signs of anaemia such as tiredness, pale skin or breathlessness
You take blood-thinning medicine and keep getting nosebleeds

name: Sinus pain or pressure
summary: Pain or pressure around the cheeks, eyes and forehead is often caused by sinusitis, usually after a cold. It is mostly viral and gets better on its own within 2 to 3 weeks.
redFlags: Swelling or redness around the eyes, double vision or difficulty moving the eye
A severe headache with a stiff neck, confusion or a rash that does not fade
Swelling of the forehead with a high temperature
urgentFlags: Feeling very unwell
Painkillers do not help or symptoms are getting worse
You have a weakened immune system, for example from chemotherapy

commonCauses.title: Viral sinusitis
commonCauses.detail: Swelling of the sinuses after a cold; the most common cause.

commonCauses.title: Bacterial sinusitis
commonCauses.detail: Less common; symptoms may be severe or get worse after starting to improve.

commonCauses.title: Allergies
commonCauses.detail: Hay fever can cause sinus congestion and pressure.

commonCauses.title: Dental infection
commonCauses.detail: An infected upper tooth can cause pain in the cheek.

selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Take over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, following the pack instructions
Hold a warm compress over your face
Rinse your nose with a saltwater solution
Ask a pharmacist about decongestant sprays or other remedies that suit you
avoid: Expecting antibiotics; most sinusitis is viral and clears without them
Using decongestant sprays for more than about a week
Smoking and smoky environments
seeDoctorIf: You are not better after 3 weeks of self-care
You are not better after 7 days of treatment from a pharmacist or doctor
You keep getting sinusitis
Symptoms are only on one side of your face

name: Loss of smell or changed sense of smell
summary: Losing your sense of smell, or things smelling different, is common after colds, flu, COVID-19 and sinus problems. It often recovers on its own within weeks, but can sometimes take longer.
redFlags: Loss of smell after a head injury with clear fluid from the nose, severe headache or confusion
Loss of smell with sudden weakness, face drooping or slurred speech
urgentFlags: Loss of smell with nosebleeds or bloody discharge on one side
Loss of smell with a blocked nose on one side only and facial swelling

commonCauses.title: Colds, flu and COVID-19
commonCauses.detail: Viral infections commonly affect smell, which usually returns over weeks.

commonCauses.title: Sinusitis and nasal polyps
commonCauses.detail: Swelling and growths can block smells reaching the top of the nose.

commonCauses.title: Allergies
commonCauses.detail: Hay fever and other allergies can reduce your sense of smell.

commonCauses.title: Ageing, smoking and some medicines
commonCauses.detail: Smell naturally weakens with age and can be affected by smoking and medicines.

commonCauses.title: Neurological conditions
commonCauses.detail: Less commonly, loss of smell can be an early sign of conditions such as Parkinson's disease.

selfCare: Try smell training: sniff a few strong scents, such as lemon, rose, clove and eucalyptus, twice a day for several months
Fit a smoke alarm and check use-by dates, since you may not smell burning or spoiled food
Treat any blocked nose with saline rinses
Stop smoking
avoid: Supplements or sprays that claim to restore smell without evidence
Overusing decongestant sprays
seeDoctorIf: Your sense of smell has not returned within 3 weeks
You have lost smell without a cold or other clear cause
Changes in smell are affecting your eating or mood
